Homemade Mustard: The search for potency

That thread gets it right. Acids will make your mustard weak and limp like Hillary's dick. For a toasty mustard start with a thick paste of the mustard flour and water and let the flavour develop for ~10 minutes (adjust for potency, longer = hotter) before adding any acidic ingredients. After that you can thin it with wine/vinegar/other acids (Orange juice concentrate makes an interesting mustard for salmon). If you are using whole mustard seed instead of flour, the reaction will take far longer, and you might want to mill it into smaller pieces first.

edit: I recommend Colman's mustard powder. It's good stuff and is consistently higher quality than anything else I've found in the grocery store.

Great advice, and succinct too! Years ago I tried a complicated German mustard recipe with tarragon and simmering but it was very disappointing. It's time to try again.

Do you know if preground (or old) mustard flour loses potency compared to freshly ground seeds?

As long as its properly sealed in a tin, it shouldn't lose much if any potency. I've had a tin of Colman's last me years and still be hot once mixed up. However, fresh ground might work better for you. It's worth trying both and seeing if the convenience outweighs any benefit. (and one downside to Colman's is the price. It's like double the price of generic stuff.)

Also, fresh ground will probably be a grittier texture than mustard flour. You may or may not prefer that.

For your question, there are numerous way exoplanets are detected - none of them are being direct viewing since as you mention we don't have anywhere near the resolution to make that possible. One method is by observing dips in the parent stars luminosity. Imagine you were some number of light years away from the solar system and had a telescope pointed right at our Sun. You would not be able to see Earth as on this sort of scale our planet is not emitting/reflecting anywhere near enough light to be visible. But you could still detect it. The way is that every 365 days (it'd actually be a range of time since we'd still be blocking light even when we weren't square on in front of you, but pinning it to a year is more clear for the sake of explanation) there would be a tiny but very predictable dip in luminosity as our planet transited across the face of the sun, from your perspective. This could tell you not only is there a planet but also its distance from its parent star since in space your distance from something you are orbiting is determined by your velocity and the relative gravities involved. Since the exoplanet's mass is negligible relative to its parent star's mass, we can determine its orbital radius based on nothing but its velocity which we can determine using its orbital period. And there are numerous other calculations you can derive as well.

None of this is too hard, but it does require at least a little bit of knowledge in astrophysics.

What this ultimately can tell us is that there's a planet orbiting the star a distance where it's possible for the planet to have surface water which makes it potentially life bearing and habitable. However, a big issue we can't yet determine so well (though the upcoming James Webb telescope should help with) is atmospheric conditions. So for instance if an atmosphere has a large amount of CO2 in it, the planet is probably a searing inferno. On the other extreme if the planet has no atmosphere it probably ranges from extreme hot to extreme cold on a daily basis. Our moon, for instance, ranges from -240F to 250F.

Wait can you explain this:

This could tell you not only is there a planet but also its distance from its parent star since in space your distance from something you are orbiting is determined by your velocity and the relative gravities involved.

Sure. The equation for orbital velocity V is:

  • V = sqrt(GM/r)

We can derive that from first principles, but you can Google for that if you're interested. I'm going to simplify and talk about the implications of the equation in general terms. In this equation G is the gravitational constant and M is the mass of the object being orbited. G never changes, and in practical scenarios neither does M. So to really get an intuitive feel for the equation we can just get rid of these values. It ends up as:

  • V2 = 1/r

So what does this tell you? It tells you first of all that your orbital radius is determined exclusively by your velocity! So if you can tell how fast something is moving, you can tell how far it is away from something. And similarly if you can tell how far away something is orbiting something at, you can tell how fast it's moving. So for instance a neat consequence of this is that all geosynchronous/geostationary satellites around a body (such as Earth) travel at the same altitude and same velocity!

The reason that's important is important is because imagine we're looking at Earth and we see something rotating around it. We can determine how often it rotates around the planet pretty easily. And if we know the radius of the planet we can then get a measurement of its orbital velocity. And once we determine its orbital velocity, we can determine its orbital radius. And the important part here is we have ways of measuring the radius of stars, even ones very far away. Add it up and we know the radius of what's being orbited, and the orbital period of what's orbiting. Thus we can determine its orbital distance!

And the equation linking this all up would be Kepler's Third law: The square of the orbital period of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit. Mathematically that'd be P2/a3 , where P is the orbital period and a is average orbital distance, is a constant for any given orbited body where the things orbiting have a negligible mass - which in the case of typical star/exoplanet relationships is true. In cases of nonnegligible mass differences the Newtonian solution or 4pi2 / GM, where M = the sum mass of both bodies, provides the constant.

It'd be nice to get a glimpse of the world we're creating but you're living at a time that ultimately may end up being the most remarkable 100 years in the history of humanity. There's a time when discovering and colonizing new planets will become mundane and about as interesting as clearing some land on Earth to build a home. We've already lived through the beginning of reuse in rocketry where we went from "That's impossible!" to "Oh, SpaceX just autonomously recovered their last 5 of 6 rockets. That's nice."

When I was a child "video phones" were literally distant future sci-fi. Now we take skyping half way around the world and chatting on a mobile device the size of your hand for granted. And in your lifetime we will almost certainly be colonizing Mars. The day the first colony is setup on Mars is one that will be memorialized for as long as the human race exists. The first human colony on another planet is something that will only happen once and will likely be the most important step towards the long term survival and expansion of our species ever.

I mean all of this is happening during your lifetime. Of course its hard to even fathom what our species will be like in 1000 years, but in terms of magnitude of accomplishments and revolutionary gains I believe you'd probably be hard pressed to find a more interesting and exciting time than the one you're currently living through. The pure good fortune of getting to live through these times is one incredibly fortunate gift...
